lesson.title: The Preamble & Key Constitutional Concepts
lesson.intro: This lesson introduces learners to the historic backdrop of the Indian Constitution, focusing on the Constituent Assembly, the visionary role of Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, and the philosophical essence of the Preamble. Students will explore why 26 November 1949 and 26 January 1950 are pivotal dates, analyse the meaning of key terms such as Sovereign, Socialist, Secular and Democratic, and understand how the Preamble reflects the basic structure doctrine. Pedagogically, the session blends narrative storytelling, chronological timelines, and simple quantitative exercises to reinforce retention and critical thinking.

keyConcepts.title: Role of the Constituent Assembly
keyConcepts.explanation: The Constituent Assembly, elected in $1946$, was responsible for drafting the Constitution, debating each article, and finally adopting the document on $\text{26 November 1949}$. It functioned like a large parliamentary committee, ensuring representation from diverse regions and communities.

keyConcepts.title: Significance of 26th November & 26th January
keyConcepts.explanation: On $\text{26 November 1949}$ the Assembly passed the final draft. After ratification by the states, the Constitution came into force on $\text{26 January 1950}$, celebrated as Republic Day, marking India's transition to a sovereign republic.

keyConcepts.title: Preamble Philosophy and Basic Structure
keyConcepts.explanation: The Preamble encapsulates the ideals of $\text{Justice}$, $\text{Liberty}$, $\text{Equality}$ and $\text{Fraternity}$. These form part of the "basic structure" that cannot be altered by any amendment, as affirmed by the Supreme Court in the Kesavananda Bharati case.

tips: Use a timeline chart to visualise the key dates (1946‑1950) for better chronological understanding.
Encourage students to paraphrase each word of the Preamble in their own language to internalise its meaning.
Link the basic structure doctrine to contemporary news articles to show its relevance today.

examples.problem: Calculate the number of years, months and days between the formation of the Constituent Assembly on $9\,\text{December}\,1946$ and the adoption of the Constitution on $26\,\text{January}\,1950$.
examples.solution: Step 1: From $9\,\text{Dec}\,1946$ to $9\,\text{Dec}\,1949$ is $3$ years.\nStep 2: From $9\,\text{Dec}\,1949$ to $26\,\text{Jan}\,1950$ is $1$ month and $17$ days.\nTherefore the total interval is $3$ years, $1$ month and $17$ days.
examples.explanation: The calculation uses simple date subtraction. First count full years, then handle the remaining months and days, ensuring correct handling of month lengths.

examples.problem: If the Preamble mentions four core values – Justice, Liberty, Equality and Fraternity – in how many different sequences can these values be arranged?
examples.solution: The number of permutations of $4$ distinct items is $4! = 4\times3\times2\times1 = 24$.\nThus there are $24$ possible arrangements.
examples.explanation: A permutation of $n$ distinct objects is given by $n!$. Here $n=4$, so $4! = 24$.

questions.prompt: In which year was the Constitution of India adopted by the Constituent Assembly? $\boxed{\;}$
questions.explanation: The Constituent Assembly passed the final draft on $\text{26 November 1949}$. Hence the correct year is $1949$.
questions.hint: Think of the date just before Republic Day 1950.

questions.prompt: The Constitution of India came into effect on which date? $\boxed{\;}$
questions.explanation: After ratification, the Constitution was enforced on $\text{26 January 1950}$, celebrated as Republic Day.
questions.hint: It coincides with the day India became a republic.

questions.prompt: Who is popularly known as the chief architect of the Indian Constitution? $\boxed{\;}$
questions.explanation: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee and is revered as the chief architect.
questions.hint: He was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee.

questions.prompt: How many members were originally elected to the Constituent Assembly in 1946? $\boxed{\;}$
questions.explanation: The first meeting of the Constituent Assembly on $9\,\text{December}\,1946$ had $389$ elected members.
questions.hint: The number is just under four hundred.

questions.prompt: Why is $26$ $\text{November}$ considered significant in the constitutional history of India? $\boxed{\;}$
questions.explanation: On $\text{26 November 1949}$ the Constituent Assembly adopted the final draft of the Constitution.
questions.hint: It precedes Republic Day by a few weeks.

questions.prompt: Which of the following words does NOT appear in the Preamble? $\boxed{\;}$
questions.explanation: The Preamble mentions Justice, Liberty, Equality and Fraternity, but not Prosperity.
questions.hint: Look for the four core values listed.

questions.prompt: Which principle is part of the "basic structure" doctrine as derived from the Preamble? $\boxed{\;}$
questions.explanation: Secularism, Federalism and Parliamentary Democracy are all recognised as components of the basic structure.
questions.hint: All three are mentioned in the Constitution’s preamble and later judicial interpretations.

questions.prompt: How many words are there in the original Preamble of the Indian Constitution? $\boxed{\;}$
questions.explanation: Counting the words in the official text yields $52$ words.
questions.hint: It is slightly more than fifty.

questions.prompt: The Preamble begins with which phrase? $\boxed{\;}$
questions.explanation: The opening words are "We, the People of India..."
questions.hint: It emphasizes popular sovereignty.

questions.prompt: Under which Act was the Constituent Assembly formed? $\boxed{\;}$
questions.explanation: The Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946 laid down the framework for the Constituent Assembly.
questions.hint: It was a mission sent by the British government.

questions.prompt: The philosophical foundation of the Preamble draws heavily from which doctrine? $\boxed{\;}$
questions.explanation: The Preamble declares India to be a "Socialist" republic, reflecting socialist ideals.
questions.hint: Look for the term that appears directly in the Preamble.

questions.prompt: On which date did the Constituent Assembly formally adopt the final draft of the Constitution? $\boxed{\;}$
questions.explanation: The final draft was adopted on $\text{26 November 1949}$ after extensive debates.
questions.hint: It is the same date celebrated as Constitution Day.

levels.title: Fundamental Rights & Writs
levels.description: Six Fundamental Rights (Articles 14 to 32) and the five constitutional writs.
subtopics: Right against Exploitation & Freedom of Religion
Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Quo-Warranto, Certiorari

lesson.title: Fundamental Rights & Constitutional Writs
lesson.intro: This lesson introduces learners to the six Fundamental Rights enshrined in Articles 14‑32 of the Indian Constitution and the five constitutional writs—Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Quo‑Warranto and Certiorari. It links constitutional provisions to everyday citizenship, encourages analytical thinking through simple quantitative exercises, and equips teachers with strategies to foster discussion, case‑study analysis and reflective writing.

keyConcepts.title: Right to Equality (Art. 14‑18)
keyConcepts.explanation: Article $14$ guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the law. Articles $15$–$18$ prohibit discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth and ensure equality of opportunity in public employment.

keyConcepts.title: Right against Exploitation & Freedom of Religion (Art. 19‑21)
keyConcepts.explanation: Articles $19$–$22$ protect freedoms of speech, assembly, movement, residence and profession, while Articles $23$–$25$ prohibit forced labour, child labour and safeguard the right to freely profess, practice and propagate religion.

keyConcepts.title: Constitutional Writs
keyConcepts.explanation: The Supreme Court and High Courts may issue five writs: \(\text{Habeas Corpus}\) (protects personal liberty), \(\text{Mandamus}\) (orders performance of a public duty), \(\text{Prohibition}\) (prevents lower courts from exceeding jurisdiction), \(\text{Quo‑Warranto}\) (questions the legality of a public office holder), and \(\text{Certiorari}\) (annuls orders of inferior courts).

tips: Use contemporary news excerpts to illustrate each fundamental right and discuss how writs have been employed in landmark cases.
Encourage students to create a mind‑map linking each article number to its core provision; visual aids reinforce retention.
Facilitate role‑play of a court scenario where students petition for a writ, reinforcing procedural understanding and civic responsibility.

examples.problem: A student wants to choose any two distinct Fundamental Rights from the six listed in Articles $14$–$32$. In how many ways can the selection be made?
examples.solution: The number of ways to choose $2$ items from $6$ is given by the combination formula $\binom{6}{2}=\frac{6\times5}{2\times1}=15$. Hence there are $15$ possible pairs of rights.
examples.explanation: We use the combination formula because the order of selection does not matter. $\binom{n}{k}=\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}$ with $n=6$, $k=2$ yields $15$.

examples.problem: A writ of Habeas Corpus is filed simultaneously in $4$ different courts. Each court can either grant (G) or deny (D) the writ. How many distinct outcome patterns are possible?
examples.solution: Each court has $2$ choices, so for $4$ courts the total outcomes are $2^{4}=16$. The possible patterns range from GGGG to DDDD.
examples.explanation: Since the decisions are independent, we multiply the number of choices: $2\times2\times2\times2=2^{4}=16$. This illustrates exponential growth with binary options.

questions.prompt: Which article of the Constitution explicitly guarantees equality before the law?
questions.explanation: Article $14$ states that the State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or equal protection of the laws, making it the correct choice.
questions.hint: Think of the first article in the Equality series.

questions.prompt: The prohibition of child labour is covered under which article?
questions.explanation: Article $23$ prohibits traffic in human beings and forced labour, including child labour, whereas Articles $24$–$26$ deal with other aspects of exploitation and religious freedom.
questions.hint: Early article in the Exploitation chapter.

questions.prompt: A citizen wishes to challenge the legality of a public office holder. Which writ is appropriate?
questions.explanation: Quo‑Warranto asks a court to determine whether a person is legally entitled to hold a public office, matching the scenario described.
questions.hint: It questions the "who" of an office.

questions.prompt: If a student can claim any of the six Fundamental Rights, in how many ways can they select exactly three distinct rights?
questions.explanation: Using the combination formula $\binom{6}{3}=\frac{6\times5\times4}{3\times2\times1}=20$. The other numeric values are incorrect.
questions.hint: Apply $\binom{n}{k}=\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}$ with $n=6$, $k=3$.

questions.prompt: Which writ is issued to compel a public authority to perform a duty it has failed to fulfill?
questions.explanation: Mandamus orders a public authority to perform a specific duty; the other writs serve different purposes.
questions.hint: Think of a command to "do" something.

questions.prompt: Article $19$ guarantees freedom of speech, but it is subject to reasonable restrictions. Which of the following is NOT a permissible restriction?
questions.explanation: Defamation is not listed among the reasonable restrictions under Article $19$; the other three are permissible.
questions.hint: Recall the five grounds listed in the Constitution.

questions.prompt: How many distinct pairs can be formed from the five constitutional writs?
questions.explanation: Number of unordered pairs from $5$ items is $\binom{5}{2}=\frac{5\times4}{2}=10$. The other options miscalculate the combination.
questions.hint: Use the combination formula with $n=5$, $k=2$.

questions.prompt: Which article provides the right to move freely throughout India?
questions.explanation: Article $19$ includes the freedom of movement throughout the territory of India as one of its six freedoms.
questions.hint: It is the first freedom listed under Article $19$.

questions.prompt: A court issues a writ to prevent a lower court from exceeding its jurisdiction. Which writ is this?
questions.explanation: Prohibition is specifically designed to stop a lower court from acting beyond its jurisdiction.
questions.hint: Think of stopping an action before it happens.

questions.prompt: If a citizen files a writ of Habeas Corpus in $3$ courts and each court can either grant or deny, how many total outcome combinations are possible?
questions.explanation: Each court has $2$ choices; for $3$ courts the total is $2^{3}=8$. The other numeric results are incorrect.
questions.hint: Apply the rule $2^{n}$ for $n$ independent binary decisions.

questions.prompt: Article $21$ guarantees the right to life and personal liberty. Which of the following best illustrates this right?
questions.explanation: Article $21$ is interpreted to include protection from arbitrary arrest and detention, whereas the other options pertain to different articles.
questions.hint: Think of personal liberty in the context of state action.

questions.prompt: Which article abolishes 'untouchability' and makes its practice an offence?
questions.explanation: Article $17$ specifically abolishes untouchability and makes its practice punishable by law.
questions.hint: It follows the Equality articles $14$–$16$.
